newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian forces clash, Amnesty expresses fears.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian forces clash, Amnesty expresses fears.

text.p: Rival forces clashed in northwest Cambodia early on Saturday and international human rights group Amnesty International expressed grave fears for the safety of hundreds of supporters of the country's ousted co-premier.

Residents in Siem Reap, 250 km (150 miles) northwest of Phnom Penh, said there was shelling in an area west of the town although the town itself, under the control of forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, remained quiet.
Forces loyal to ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh have been attacking Hun Sen's troops in the area in an attempt to cut the town off, military officials loyal to Hun Sen said.
Residents of Siem Reap, near the famed Angkor Wat temple complex, said the shelling began about an hour after dawn and lasted some 20 minutes.
There were no reports of casualties and military officials in the area were not immediately available for comment.

In a letter obtained by Reuters on Saturday, London-based Amnesty International expressed serious concerns about the fate of hundreds of soldiers and officials of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party believed to have been captured by Hun Sen's forces.

"We hold grave fears for the safety of the hundreds of FUNCINPEC soldiers and officials believed to be in the custody of your forces," Amnesty secretary general Pierre Sane said in an open letter to Hun Sen.
Amnesty said it was deeply concerned for the safety of politicians, journalists and activists linked to FUNCINPEC and two smaller parties allied to the royalists.

"We urge you to clarify immediately and publicly the status and welfare of all those being held, provide guarantees for their safety and fair treatment and afford access to them by independent monitors," Sane said. Sane also condemned the reported summary execution of officials from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party.

Hun Sen's officials confirmed the arrest and subsequent execution of senior FUNCINPEC member Ho Sok, a secretary of state at the interior ministry. Hun Sen later said he regretted Ho Sok's death and said he had ordered and an investigation to find out who was responsible.
A newspaper which supports Hun Sen later reported the suicide of FUNCINPEC intelligence officer, Chao Sambath, although government officials have not confirmed his death.
Ho Sok and Chao Sambath were among four senior royalists who Hun Sen said were responsible for last week's fighting in Phnom Penh which left at least 58 dead and up to 200 wounded.
In an apparent reference to the brutality of Cambodia's "killing fields" regime, Amnesty's Sane urged Hun Sen to halt alleged human rights abuses.

"You know only too well the spectre of gross human rights violations that haunts Cambodia to this day," he said. More than one million Cambodians died under the brutal Maoist Khmer Rouge rule from 1975 to 1979.
The other two royalists identified by Hun Sen were Ranariddh's top military man, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, and the prince's chief security officer, Serey Kosal.

General Nhiek Bun Chhay fled from Phnom Penh as Hun Sen's forces took control of the city and its outskirts on Sunday. His whereabouts were not known but there have been rumours he was captured by Hun Sen's troops. Serey Kosal is believed to have fled to northwestern Cambodia.
